analysis.one_liner: Bans union agreements requiring workers to join or pay dues to a union.
analysis.headline: The National Right-to-Work Act, which would have barred union dues requirements in all 50 states, attracted 112 cosponsors — every one a Republican — but never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend two federal labor laws — the National Labor Relations Act and the Railway Labor Act — to strike the provisions that let employers and unions sign agreements requiring workers to join or pay dues to a union as a condition of employment. That would make "right-to-work" rules national: today at least 27 states already ban these agreements on their own. The practical effect would be that unions, which must represent every worker in a workplace they cover, could no longer require the workers they represent to contribute dues.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who would rather not pay dues to a union would keep their jobs and the wages and benefits the union negotiates without contributing anything. Employers would gain too: unions with thinner treasuries have less money to organize, bargain, and file grievances, which shifts bargaining power toward management.

how_it_helps.text: A worker who does not want to join a union or pay dues could keep the job regardless of any agreement between the employer and the union — today, in the roughly half of states without their own right-to-work law, such agreements can make joining or paying a condition of employment.
Sponsors framed the bill as protecting the 'free choice of individual employees' to refrain from union activity, not just to join one.
It would put every state on the same footing: at least 27 states already prohibit compulsory union membership, and the bill would extend that rule to the rest of the country through federal law.

analysis.who_pays: Union members and the unions themselves. Unions are legally required to represent every worker in a unit they cover, so a national ban on dues agreements would let many workers receive union-negotiated pay and benefits without paying in — shrinking the dues that fund bargaining, grievance handling, and organizing. States with these laws generally have lower union membership and weaker wage growth for the workers affected. Railroad and airline workers, covered by the Railway Labor Act, would be subject to the same ban.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes a union's ability to require contributions but not its legal duty to represent every worker in the bargaining unit, creating free riders who get negotiated wages and contract protections without paying for them — which drains the funds unions use to bargain and enforce contracts.

Right-to-work laws in the states are associated with lower union membership, and weaker unions generally mean less bargaining power and slower wage growth for workers; the bill would apply that regime nationwide rather than leaving it to state choice.

The good-faith case for it — that no worker should be forced to financially support an organization they disagree with — is a real individual-liberty claim, but it is bought at the cost of the shared funding that makes collective bargaining workable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The individual-freedom benefit is real but narrow: the workers it directly helps are those who object to paying dues in workplaces with union security agreements. The cost is broad, because it defunds the unions that bargain for millions of workers, including workers who never pay dues, and shifts bargaining leverage toward employers. Weighing the two, the bill's main effect would be to weaken organized labor nationally, with the choice-based gains for individual workers much smaller than the collective losses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee's majority never took it up, so it died quietly when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Wilson of South Carolina introduced the National Right-to-Work Act on February 24, 2021, joined by 58 original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
Over the following months it accumulated 112 cosponsors, every one of them a Republican — roughly half the House Republican conference — but no hearing, markup, or floor action followed.

The action history shows only two entries for the entire two-year Congress: introduction and the committee referral. No further action was ever taken, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Unions and their members came out ahead: union security agreements remain lawful in the states that allow them, and unions keep the dues base the bill would have eliminated. Employers hoping to operate under a national right-to-work regime got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Joe Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the National Right-to-Work Act to strike the federal provisions allowing union security agreements.

for.name: 112 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; all 112 were Republicans, though none could get the bill a hearing or a vote.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor majority
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving the bill to expire.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.role: Majority leadership controlling the House floor calendar
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with Democrats holding the majority, the bill had no path forward without their scheduling.

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 112 cosponsors was a Republican, and it went nowhere in the Democrat-controlled committee that would have had to move it.

industries.note: The bill's central target: unions would lose the ability to require dues from the workers they are obligated to represent, cutting their funding for bargaining and organizing. In this bill the unions' interest runs with the workers whose pay and contract enforcement depend on that funding, though supporters argue individual workers who object to dues would gain.

A union that cannot collect dues from the workers it represents is a weaker bargaining opponent, so the bill would shift leverage toward employers on wages, benefits, and working conditions. That gain comes directly at the expense of the workers' collective voice.
